name: Maya Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying civil engineering. Mornings are lectures on structures and surveying, and every second Friday we do fieldwork measuring a site with a total station. I have a room in a student flat near campus, which my parents pay for. They run a farm machinery dealership back home, three hours away, and I go back most weekends.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fieldwork, and I like the way a bridge has to be right. What wears me out is the pace of the maths and living far from home. On Sundays I go to the church near campus, and it keeps me steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I thought would happen. I'd tell my flatmates that people have been predicting the end of work since I was a child. I don't post anything, but I'd mention it at church coffee, where my views are not unusual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel settled. Civil engineering is real work with real concrete, and it won't go away. I'd still worry about finding a good placement, since my results are average and I'm not good at selling myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd go to every site visit, keep my notes by hand, and apply to a local contractor for the summer. I'd also go home on weekends to work in the dealership, because I learn a lot there about machines and customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the kind of world I like, where what you know and what you do still counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools. Is that a decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's partly a decision. I prefer to learn things properly first. I feel that tools that give you the answer take away the part where you learn, and I don't want to be an engineer who can't check a beam myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a plateau mean for the family business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dealership would carry on the same. My dad would still be selling tractors and my brother Joaquim would still be fixing them. Farming doesn't change just because the news says it will.

say: I'd say that's what I **expected**: people have predicted the end of work for years.
I'd mention it over **church coffee**, where my views are common.
think: Civil engineering is real work with **real concrete** and won't go away.
I'm still worried about a **placement**, since I'm average and bad at selling myself.
do: Go to every **site visit** and keep notes by hand.
Apply to a local **contractor** for the summer and work weekends at the dealership.
feel: **Calm**: a world where what you know still counts.
S0.quote: Farming doesn't change just because the news says it will.
fieldNote: She chooses not to use AI because she wants to **learn properly** first.
Traditional values show in church and family business anchors.
Worry is placement and self-presentation, not AI.

steps.text: Go to every site visit and keep field notes by hand
Apply to a local contractor for the summer
Work weekends in the family dealership

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of noise, but some of it is real. I'd tell friends to keep working hard and not wait for anyone to rescue them. At church I'd say we need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think office jobs will change first, like accounting and drawing and bookkeeping. Surveying and building should hold up better. I worry that my course trains a lot of drafting that software could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the contractors I know about which skills they're hiring for. I'd try to get time on site, not only in the office. I'd also finally learn the drawing software well, because I'd rather learn one tool properly than a lot of tools badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like change that I haven't chosen. But I'd try not to show it to my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your family's work would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dealership's bookkeeping and ordering, certainly. My aunt Beatriz does the invoices, and software can already do most of that. The tractors still need people to fix them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should help people whose jobs disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family and the community first, then employers who train people, and only then the government. I don't believe in handouts as the main answer, but I'd make an exception if people have truly lost their work.

say: I'd say there's a lot of **noise**, but some is real.
I'd tell friends to keep **working hard** and at church say we should look after each other.
think: Office tasks like drafting and **bookkeeping** go first, while building holds up.
My course trains **drafting** that software could do.
do: Ask contractors which **skills** they hire for and seek time on site.
Learn the **drawing software** properly, one tool at a time.
feel: **Uneasy**, since I don't like change I didn't choose.
S1.quote: Family and the community first, then employers who train people, and only then the government.
fieldNote: She wants **practical** training and community support before state help.
Names concrete family tasks that software already covers.
Will adopt one tool only, and properly.

steps.text: Ask local contractors which skills they hire for
Spend more weekends on site rather than in the office
Learn the drawing software properly this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we aren't ready, and nobody in charge is either. I'd tell people not to panic but to look after their families first. I'd speak at church about helping neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried. In two years, the thinking part of my degree would be done by AI, and I'd graduate into that. Hands-on work has about three more years, so I'd go where the work is physical and local.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move toward practical skills and an apprenticeship. I'd ask my father whether I can train in the dealership workshop, learning to repair machines. I'd keep the degree going, because it's a qualification, and use my site experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like the ground is moving, and I'm someone who likes it firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your father about the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him that the business may be what saves us, since machines and farms need people for longer. I'd offer to come home sooner and help. He'd probably tell me to finish my degree first, and I'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about church or community?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help organise a group that helps neighbours who lose work, like a food store and a job board. That's what a church should do. I'd rather do that than argue online.

say: I'd say **nobody** in charge is ready either.
I'd tell people to look after their families first and speak at church about helping **neighbours**.
think: In two years **AI** would do the thinking part of my degree.
Hands-on work has about three more years, so I'd go where the work is **physical and local**.
do: Ask my father to train me in the dealership **workshop**.
Start a job board and food store with the **church** group.
feel: **Anxious**, like the ground is moving under someone who likes it firm.
S2.quote: Hands-on work has about three more years, so I'd go where the work is physical and local.
fieldNote: She turns to **family and church**, not to government.
The dealership workshop is her chosen fallback.
Keeps the degree as a qualification, since employers will still ask for it.

steps.text: Ask Dad to train me in the dealership workshop
Offer to come home sooner and help in the business
Set up a job board and food store at church
Keep going with the degree for the qualification

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a warning that we can act on. I'd tell friends to be ready to work with their hands as well as their heads. At church I'd say hard work and community will see us through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel uneasy but steady. I'd graduate in 2029, then have a couple of years working on real sites before the big change. Robots come around 2034, which gives the practical trades a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and work for a local contractor for a few years, and keep working weekends in the dealership. I'd also take a course in machine repair. I'd save from my part-time wage, since I want to be able to help if the dealership needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel better if I had a plan on paper, so I'd make one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you use five years for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I can do the engineering degree and learn the machines too, so I have two ways to earn. That feels sensible to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move home earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it. If the dealership needed me, I'd go. Otherwise I'd stay near a site and learn what a good engineer does.

say: I'd say it's a **warning** we can act on.
I'd tell friends to be ready to work with their **hands** as well as their heads.
think: I'd get a couple of years on **real sites** before the big change.
Robots arrive around 2034, which gives **practical trades** a long time.
do: Finish the degree, work for a local **contractor** and keep dealership weekends.
Take a **machine repair** course and save from my wage.
feel: **Uneasy**, but a plan on paper would help.
S3.quote: With five years, I can do the engineering degree and learn the machines too, so I have two ways to earn.
fieldNote: Her plan is **two ways to earn**: engineering and machine repair.
Savings are aimed at helping the family business if needed.
Makes plans on paper to manage anxiety.

steps.text: Work for a local contractor after graduating
Take a machine repair course in the dealership workshop
Save part of my wage in case the dealership needs help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a good amount of time. I'd tell friends to build a trade and a family. At church I'd probably just say thank you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be quite calm. I'd be 28 with a career, a bit of money and maybe a family. Ten years is time to build something solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work, and help with the business, and I'd learn any new tool that proves its worth. I'd save and maybe buy a small house near home. I'd keep my faith and routines, which have always helped me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the kind of time where you can live your life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, do you worry at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, about whether prices and farming change in ways I can't see. But mostly I'd trust that people adapt, as they always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to hand on to your own children one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to hand on a skill, a trade and a good name, because those are the things nobody can switch off. That's what my father gave my brother and me.

say: I'd say that's a good amount of **time**.
I'd tell friends to build a **trade and a family**.
think: I'd be 28 with a **career**, some money and maybe a family.
Ten years is time to build something **solid**.
do: Finish the degree, work, and help with the **business**.
Save for a small house near **home**, and learn tools only when they prove worth.
S4.quote: I'd want to hand on a skill, a trade and a good name, because those are the things nobody can switch off.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on **faith**, family and a trade.
She adopts tools only when they prove their worth.
Goal is to hand on a skill and a good name.

steps.text: Finish the degree and work near home
Save towards a small house near the family
Help in the dealership alongside my brother Joaquim

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture. Everything would change at once and we'd have no time to teach our families. What would help is practical training, employers who give apprenticeships, and communities that look after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of hard work or of change itself. I'm afraid of change that arrives before anyone has had time to teach their children what it means.

headlineQuote: I'm afraid of change that arrives before anyone has had time to teach their children what it means.
portrait: **Maya** is 18, studies civil engineering, and her parents, who run a farm machinery dealership, pay for her room near campus.
She avoids AI tools on purpose, wants to learn properly first, and goes home most weekends.
She is calm at a plateau or a decade, uneasy in the middle cases, and anxious only with a two-year warning.
She trusts family, church and apprenticeships over handouts, and her fallback is the dealership workshop.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most: change before anyone can teach their children what it means.
whatWouldHelp: Practical **training**, employers who offer apprenticeships, and communities that look after each other.
